9.11.4 Mortality
Maternal mortality, child/adolescent mortality, and infant mortality are summarized using rates and, where available, comparisons to regional and state benchmarks Figure 9.88, Figure 9.89, Figure 9.90. Maternal mortality (rate per 100,000 live births) for 2018-2021 declined from 39.1 in 2018 to 12.3 in 2021 Figure 9.88. In the most recent year displayed (2021), Orange County’s maternal mortality rate (12.3) was lower than the Mid-Hudson region (20.7) and both NYS excluding NYC (22.6) and NYS overall (21.6) Figure 9.88.
Child and adolescent mortality (rate per 100,000 population aged 10–19 years) is presented for 2018–2021 Figure 9.89. Orange County’s rate fluctuated across the period, with 17.6 in 2018 and 18.8 in 2021 Figure 9.89. In 2021, Orange County’s mortality rate among youth aged 10–19 (18.8) exceeded the Mid-Hudson rate (21.9) but was lower than NYS excluding NYC (24.1) and NYS overall (23.6) as displayed in the figure Figure 9.89.
For 2020–2022, Orange County’s infant mortality rate was 3.6 per 1,000 births, compared with 4.6 in NYS excluding NYC and 4.2 in NYS overall Figure 9.90. Disparities by race/ethnicity were present within Orange County: Non-Hispanic Black infants had the highest infant mortality rate (5.6 per 1,000), compared with Non-Hispanic White (3.2), Hispanic (3.0), and Non-Hispanic Asian/Pacific Islander (2.6) Figure 9.90.

9.11.5 Prenatal Care
Prenatal care utilization is summarized using measures of early prenatal care, late/no prenatal care, and adequate prenatal care Table 9.108, Table 9.109, Figure 9.91, Figure 9.92, Figure 9.93, Figure 9.94, Figure 9.95, Figure 9.96, Figure 9.97. In Orange County, the percentage of births with early prenatal care was 68.9% in 2020, declined to 63.9% in 2021, and returned to 68.9% in 2023 Table 9.108. Differences by race/ethnicity were evident in 2023: Non-Hispanic White mothers had a higher percentage of births with early prenatal care (75.2%) compared with Hispanic (58.0%) and Black Alone (62.8%) Table 9.108.
Births with Late or No Prenatal Care are also presented for 2020–2023 Table 9.109. Orange County’s percentage of births with late or no prenatal care increased from 5.0% in 2020 to 6.6% in 2023 Table 9.109. In 2023, disparities were observed by race/ethnicity: Black Alone births had 11.5% late/no prenatal care and Hispanic births had 10.1%, compared with 4.1% among Non-Hispanic White births Table 9.109. Geographic variation was also shown; in 2023, late/no prenatal care was 12.2% in zip 12550 compared with 3.0% in zip 10950 Table 9.109.
Adequate prenatal care is presented as a percent for 2018–2021 in the figure and includes regional and state comparisons Figure 9.97. Orange County’s percent of births with adequate prenatal care increased from 63.2% in 2018 to 66.1 in 2021 Figure 9.97. In 2021, Orange County’s value (66.1) was lower than the Mid-Hudson region (72.2) and both NYS excluding NYC (78.2) and NYS overall (75.3) Figure 9.97.

9.11.6 Birth Outcomes: Premature Birth and Low Birthweight
The percentage of premature births in Orange County was 8.5% in 2020 and 8.0% in 2023 Table 9.117. In 2023, premature birth was higher among Black Alone births (13.8%) compared with Non-Hispanic White births (6.1%) Table 9.117. Zip code stratifications also showed variation; in 2023, premature births were 12.4% in zip 10940 compared with 3.8% in zip 10950 Table 9.117. A multi-year race/ethnicity comparison for 2020–2022 showed Orange County’s overall premature birth percentage at 8.4%, lower than NYS excluding NYC (9.5%) and NYS overall (9.5%), while within Orange County the highest burden remained among Non-Hispanic Black births (14.9%) Figure 9.99.
The percentage of low birthweight births was 6.9% in 2020 and 6.6% in 2023 Table 9.118. In 2023, low birthweight was higher among Black Alone births (14.0%) than among Non-Hispanic White births (5.4%) Table 9.118. Zip code stratifications showed additional variation; in 2023, low birthweight births were 11.8% in zip 10940 compared with 3.0% in zip 10950 Table 9.118. In the multi-year period 2020–2022, Orange County’s overall low birthweight percentage was 7.1%, lower than NYS excluding NYC (8.0%) and NYS overall (8.4%), with the highest burden among Non-Hispanic Black births (13.4%) Figure 9.101.

title: 10  Health Behaviors
text:
10.1 Substance Use
Health behaviors include the actions and habits that influence an individual’s health status, longevity, and risk of preventable disease and injury. This section summarizes key measures across two domains—Substance Use and Injury Prevention & Safety—using the tables and figures listed below.
Substance use patterns reflect both individual behavior and broader community conditions that shape risk exposure, access to treatment, and the likelihood of adverse outcomes. In Orange County, substance-use–related indicators show improvement across several acute-care burden measures, while also demonstrating persistent concentration of overdose mortality by age and sex and ongoing youth access patterns driven largely by social sourcing.

title: 10  Health Behaviors

10.1.1 Hospitalizations
Substance use hospitalizations (ED visits) and neonatal abstinence show a decline over the years. ED visit rates for diagnoses related to any drug use declined from 194.5 per 100,000 (2019) to 178.0 (2022), after a higher value in 2020 Figure 10.1. Opioid-related ED visit rates also declined from 175.5 (2019) to 114.1 (2022) Figure 10.2. Neonatal abstinence syndrome rates decreased from 9.2 per 1,000 births (2019) to 6.7 (2022) Figure 10.3.

10.1.2 Controlled Substance Prescribing Patterns
Controlled substance prescribing indicators trend downward overall, with one prescribing-risk metric increasing modestly. The opioid prescribing rate declined from 292.5 per 1,000 person-years (2021) to 261.8 (2024) Figure 10.4, and benzodiazepine prescribing decreased from 245.1 (2021) to 221.3 (2024) Figure 10.6. Co-prescribing overlap (opioid + benzodiazepine) declined from 9.1% (2021) to 8.0% (2024) (Figure 127). In contrast, the share of opioid-naïve patients receiving a 7+ day supply increased from 14.9% (2021) to 15.8% (2024) Figure 10.5. Treatment-related prescribing measures show buprenorphine prescribing declining from 610.5 (2021) to 499.6 (2024) Figure 10.7, while the percentage receiving continuous buprenorphine increased from 71.3% (2021) to 74.2% (2024) Figure 10.8.

10.1.3 Youth Substance Use and Perception
Youth perception and use patterns show clear grade gradients for several substances, while marijuana stands out for lower perceived risk and measurable current use. Perceived “moderate/great risk” increases by grade for alcohol and cigarettes (e.g., cigarettes rise from 76.1% in grade 8 to 87.6% in grade 12), while marijuana shows lower perceived risk overall and declines by grade (65.0% grade 8 to 54.7% grade 12) Figure 10.9. Lifetime use also rises by grade across multiple substances; for example, lifetime alcohol use increases from 12.4% (grade 8) to 46.8% (grade 12), and lifetime marijuana use from 7.0% to 17.3% Table 10.9. Past-30-day use is lower in absolute terms but identifies ongoing behaviors, including energy drink use (31.1% total), alcohol (13.0%), marijuana (5.4%), and nicotine vaping (5.4%) Table 10.10. Among students reporting marijuana use, the most frequently reported access was getting it from someone under age 21 (49.2%), followed by someone age 21+ (21.5%) and a party (21.5%), with additional access from home without permission (18.0%) or with permission (10.6%) Table 10.11.

10.2 Injury Prevention & Safety
Injury prevention and safety behaviors reflect the decisions and environmental conditions that influence injury risk, avoidable hospitalization, and preventable mortality. Indicators in Orange County show differences by race/ethnicity, age, sex, and geography, with additional burden from falls among older adults and measurable adolescent vulnerability for self-inflicted injury hospitalizations.

10.2.1 Unintentional Injury
Unintentional hospitalization and mortality show clear subgroup and geographic differences. Unintentional injury hospitalization rates (2020–2022 average) were 70.1 per 10,000 in Orange County, with variation by race/ethnicity (e.g., Non-Hispanic White: 68.4; Hispanic: 42.0; Non-Hispanic Asian: 26.6) Figure 10.15. Unintentional injury mortality increases markedly with age; for example, the 85+ age group reached 455.8 per 100,000 in 2022 Figure 10.17, Table 10.16. Across the four city ZIP codes shown, the 2020–2023 average ranged from 68.2 (ZIP 10940) to 159.5 (ZIP 12550) Figure 10.18, Table 10.16. Age-adjusted injury mortality rates, stratified by sex, show higher mortality among males than females across all years shown Figure 10.19.

title: 12  Health Summit
text:
Skip to main content




The OC Health Summit was held on October 28, 2025, with a record turnout of 140 attendees, including hospitals, healthcare providers, community-based organizations, and academia, to review the current state of health in OC. This year’s theme, “From Data to Decisions: Shaping Orange County’s Health Future,” emphasized turning data collection and reporting into actionable decisions that drive engagement, improvement, and awareness of health outcomes.
An overview of the most recently available data was provided to participants, covering:

2025 Community Partner Survey Results and focus groups data overview
Community Health Survey results were given
Preliminary results from the 2025 Community Asset Survey
Hanlon Method overview
Data Summary across assessments

12.0.1 Keynote Presentation
A presentation by Dr. Marisa Donnelly, PhD (Your Local Epidemiologist), examined how to reimagine public health in Orange County by centering trust, clear communication, and genuine community engagement across the full cycle of assessment, prioritization, action, and feedback. She emphasized that public health is inherently local, seen in challenges such as vaccine hesitancy, maternal-health gaps, and overdose spikes.
Dr. Donnelly recommended strategies that included meeting residents where they are (leveraging social media more effectively and amplifying positive, human messages), moving beyond one-way information to two-way engagement (timely responses, listening for concerns and rumors, and inviting feedback), and treating trust as an ongoing practice by communicating early, often, and with acknowledged uncertainty. Dr. Donnelly described a transition from top-down, linear models to decentralized, community-anchored networks that rely on trusted messengers (e.g., teachers, faith leaders) and encouraged practitioners to “play offense” by anticipating narratives, learning from what worked and what didn’t, and forging new partnerships (e.g., collaborations between parent influencers and epidemiologists). Building on the prior CHIP focus areas of reducing food insecurity, increasing cancer screening, and decreasing opioid deaths. She challenged participants to bridge the gap between priorities and practice by elevating community-defined needs, discontinuing approaches that don’t serve residents, and strengthening health literacy and social media curricula so people can better discern credible information while providers focus on measurable outcomes, independent of political influence. Q&A highlighted algorithmic realities (content that spreads anger), the importance of staying audience-focused rather than partisan, the need for patient–clinician partnerships in an era of rapid information access, and emerging research efforts that integrate substance use, violence prevention, and HIV services to improve local impact.



Figure 12.1: Dr Marisa Donnelly presenting to community partners, OC Health Summit 2025








12.0.2 Data Update
An Orange County Health Data Update was presented to participants, summarizing statewide changes and local indicators that will guide the next planning cycle. The New York State Prevention Agenda 2025–2030 elevates social determinants of health and extends the Community Health Improvement Plan (CHIP) to a six-year cycle, with at least one county priority required in the SDOH domain. Locally, regional assessments will post soon; the Orange County Community Health Assessment (CHA) is slated for completion by December, and the new six-year CHIP is due in June 2026. This work is informed by an expanded evidence base, including the 2024 Community Health Survey, Community Partner and Community Asset surveys, focus groups with underrepresented residents, and ongoing updates from the Health Equity Dashboard.
Key findings underscore the need for equity-focused, measurable strategies. In 2023, the leading causes of death were cardiovascular disease, cancer, and unintentional injury; nearly half of the deaths were premature, exceeding the statewide rate. Economic strain remains pronounced, with widening food insecurity among residents earning under $25,000, and many households spending at least half their income on housing. Cancer mortality is the highest in the Mid-Hudson region. It is the eighth worst in New York State, and about 20% above the state rate, while essential immunizations by age two trail regional and state (excluding NYC) benchmarks. Together, these results reinforce a CHIP that centers SDOH, pairs clinical and community strategies, and tracks progress over the six-year horizon.



Figure 12.2: Jackie Lawler presenting to community partners, OC Health Summit 2025








12.0.3 Priority Area Voting
Summit participants were then invited to vote on the health indicators where they felt Orange County could make the greatest impact, using the results of the Hanlon prioritization as a guide. The following indicators were included:

Cancer
Childhood Immunizations
Childhood Obesity
Diabetes
Food Security
Infant Mortality
Opioid Burden
Physical Activity
Prenatal Care
Suicide

Each participant received three adhesive dots to place on the indicators they believed should be prioritized. This dot-voting process allowed partners to visually express their collective judgment and quickly identify areas of shared concern. When the votes were tallied, three indicators emerged as clear priorities: Food Security ranked first with 80 votes, Cancer ranked second with 42 votes, and Opioid Burden ranked third with 35 votes. These selections guided the subsequent focus of planning and discussion for the Community Health Improvement Plan.



Figure 12.3: Summit participants voting on selected health indicator, OC Health Summit 2025








12.0.4 Forces of Change Discussion
A Forces of Change Assessment (FOCA) discussion was held to better understand the trends, factors, and events that are shaping health in Orange County and influencing how effectively the local public health system can respond. Partners emphasized that virtually all of the county’s priority health issues are rooted in broader economic conditions. Participants noted that Orange County’s food system is heavily tied to federal policies and funding streams, including the USDA. Ongoing uncertainty around federal government operations and potential shutdowns was identified as a major threat to school meal programs, food pantries, and soup kitchens across New York State. These economic and policy forces were seen as foundational drivers behind food insecurity and many of the county’s other health priorities.
Access to prevention and treatment services emerged as another dominant theme. Partners highlighted the need to strengthen colorectal cancer screening and survivorship support for residents at high risk of recurrence. They also underscored the importance of coordination and patient follow-up, as well as education and advocacy, to ensure that individuals can move more seamlessly through the continuum of care. In the behavioral health space, participants described a critical gap in detoxification services, particularly on weekends, and called for opening and streamlining access so that people in crisis can enter care more fluidly. Stigma surrounding substance use disorder, mental health, suicide, and help-seeking was identified as a persistent barrier that discourages residents from reaching out for support.
Participants also noted that Orange County has a wide range of resources and programs that many residents simply do not know exist. Efforts such as Hope Not Handcuffs, Welcome Orange (with an upcoming orientation at the end of November), and various local coalitions were highlighted as important assets that could be leveraged more fully. Partners suggested designating staff or partners to proactively identify evidence-based resources and share them directly with clients, rather than waiting for people to seek them out. The underutilization of the 311 and 988 lines was cited as a missed opportunity: both numbers are “full of resources and ready to share,” and attendees emphasized that “every day a phone call saves someone’s life.”
Several forces of change were tied to specific populations and cross-jurisdictional issues. The political environment was recognized as a stressor that can negatively impact mental health and community well-being. Veterans were identified as a key group needing more focused outreach and engagement. Although many veterans are eligible for free health coverage, partners reported that some are reluctant to use services because they fear taking resources away from others. With more than 20,000 veterans in Orange County and only about 6,000 currently served, this was viewed as a significant gap and an opportunity to improve trust, communication, and navigation. Participants also noted substantial crossovers with neighboring Sullivan County, underscoring the importance of continued regional collaboration to address shared challenges and serve individuals who move across county lines.
Finally, partners stressed the importance of human connection as a protective factor in the face of these forces of change. Beyond programs and hotlines, residents often need someone who can “hold their hand or sit with them” in the hospital, in a nursing home, or at home during difficult times. The FOCA discussion reinforced that education, advocacy, coordination, and compassionate accompaniment, combined with stronger cross-sector networks, are essential to helping Orange County residents navigate complex systems, reduce the impact of economic and social stressors, and improve health across all priority areas. 


12.0.5 Selected Priority Areas Discussion
After the FOCA, a focused discussion was held on the three health indicators identified as top priorities by summit participants: food security, cancer, and opioid burden.
For food security, partners in the network of hospitals and community-based efforts already have systems in place to support residents experiencing food insecurity. Examples included providing tailored bags of food for patients and families at discharge, accommodating dietary and clinical needs, and integrating safe sleep education and equipment into discharge planning for families with newborns. Community organizations and coalitions are working to ensure food reaches residents where they are, including those who are homebound or socially isolated, and there is an ongoing need for volunteers to assist with distribution and outreach. Participants also highlighted opportunities to connect food assistance with education on mental health and other supportive services.
In examining the cancer health indicator, participants emphasized prevention, early detection, and survivorship. Mobile screening efforts were identified as an important strategy to reach residents in their own communities, especially individuals facing transportation or access barriers. Alcohol-related cancers associated with binge drinking were raised as a concern, highlighting the need for integrated messaging around substance use and cancer risk. Rising colorectal cancer rates among younger adults, including women, were discussed, along with the importance of promoting earlier cancer screenings and increasing awareness of available health coverage. Participants also identified the need to expand survivorship supports and patient navigation to help residents move more effectively through screening, diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up.
The opioid burden discussion centered on understanding root causes and strengthening the response. Participants raised questions about how broader substance use trends, including changing policies and norms, may be influencing opioid use in the community. There was broad agreement that additional resources must be directed toward mental health services, given that untreated mental health needs often underline substance use. Reducing stigma around opioid use was identified as essential, as stigma often prevents individuals and families from seeking help. Partners emphasized bringing education, screening, and support directly into the communities they serve, recognizing that taking the first step to get care is often the most difficult part of the recovery journey.
Taken together, these discussions around food security, cancer, and opioid burden underscored several cross-cutting themes: integrating clinical and community-based services, expanding outreach to underserved and isolated residents, reducing stigma, and strengthening navigation and follow-up across the continuum of care. Insights from this session will directly inform the development of goals, objectives, and strategies in the Community Health Improvement Plan, ensuring that Orange County’s efforts remain grounded in both data and community experience.

title: 13  Community Input
text: 13.1 Focus Groups and Key Informant Interviews

title: 13  Community Input
text:
13.1.1 Overview
As part of the Community Health Assessment (CHA) process, the Orange County Department of Health engaged directly with community partners and residents from historically underrepresented and underserved populations to gain a deeper understanding of the factors influencing health and well-being across the county. Focus groups were conducted with individuals experiencing homelessness, LGBTQIA+ community members, Veterans, and representatives from an African American faith-based organization. These groups were selected to ensure that perspectives from populations disproportionately affected by health inequities were meaningfully incorporated into the assessment process.
Participants were asked a consistent set of core questions designed to explore lived experiences and community-identified priorities, including:

What does a healthy life look like to you?
What are some of the biggest challenges to living a healthy life?
Despite these challenges, what is currently helping you live a healthy life?
What about living in Orange County is good for you and your family’s health?
What about living in Orange County makes it challenging to be healthy?
Do you feel there are any resources that are lacking in Orange County that would be helpful to achieving a healthier life?

These conversations provided critical qualitative insight into lived experiences, systemic barriers, and community-identified priorities that are not always captured through quantitative data alone. Collectively, the findings highlight how social, economic, and structural factors shape health outcomes and underscore the importance of community-informed approaches to improving health equity.
While focus group participation varied by population, it is worth noting that the Veterans’ focus group had a limited number of participants. Because this group was small, the themes should be used carefully and seen as examples rather than representing all Veterans. Even so, these findings give important insight into their experiences and were included to make sure Veteran voices were part of the assessment.


13.1.2 Themes Identified Across Focus Groups
Despite differences in lived experience and population-specific needs, several common themes emerged consistently across all focus groups. Participants across groups described health as being deeply influenced by access to care, housing stability, transportation, affordability, mental health services, and the availability of culturally responsive and affirming services. Many participants emphasized that navigating complex systems, healthcare, housing, social services, and social benefits was itself a significant barrier to health. The table below summarizes the primary cross-cutting themes identified across focus groups Table 13.1.

13.1.3 Focus Group Summaries


13.1.4 Unhoused Residents (Newburgh Ministry)
Participants experiencing homelessness described health as inseparable from stability, dignity, and access to essential resources. A healthy life was defined not only by physical and mental well-being, but by the ability to access consistent primary care, reliable transportation, and nutritious food. Many participants described accessing primary care as stressful and, at times, traumatic, noting that scheduling appointments often requires advance planning that is difficult without stable housing or transportation. The loss of mobile medical services, such as on-site medical vans and regular nurse practitioner visits, was identified as a significant gap in care access. Housing instability was consistently identified as the most significant barrier to health. Participants described unsafe and unstable living conditions, limited communication and follow-up from caseworkers, and policies that penalize individuals for gaining employment. Several participants explained that earning a modest income led to sudden discharge from assistance programs without sufficient time to secure stable housing, perpetuating a cycle of instability and homelessness. Transportation barriers affected nearly all aspects of daily life, including access to medical appointments, transportation to Social Security offices, appearing on court dates, and transportation to employment. Participants reported long wait times for medical transportation and limited options for traveling between municipalities, often resulting in missed appointments and delayed care. Access to food was also identified as a challenge, particularly during transitions when emergency SNAP benefits are delayed. Despite these challenges, participants highlighted the role of community-based organizations as essential support. Limited access to computers and internet services through libraries was also cited as a critical resource for navigating systems and maintaining communication. Participants emphasized that improvements in housing stability, transportation coordination, and follow-through within social service systems would substantially improve health outcomes for unhoused residents.


13.1.5 LGBTQIA+ Community Members
LGBTQIA+ participants described a healthy life as one that includes both physical and mental well-being, supported by affirming, accessible, and culturally competent healthcare. Access to trained medical providers, particularly those knowledgeable in LGBTQIA+ and gender-affirming care, was identified as essential. Many participants reported needing to travel outside of Orange County, often to New York City or Syracuse, to receive appropriate primary and specialized care. The most significant challenges identified included provider unwillingness to treat LGBTQIA+ patients, limited access to affirming housing, food, and employment, and a broader community climate that can feel unwelcoming or unsafe. Participants noted that visible symbols of intolerance contributed to feelings of exclusion and fear, particularly for LGBTQIA+ youth who lack safe and affirming spaces. Insurance coverage gaps, especially for individuals who have aged out of parental coverage, further compound barriers to care. Despite these challenges, participants highlighted the importance of the small number of affirming providers within Orange County, noting that even a single trusted provider can have a meaningful impact on health and well-being. Supportive individuals and informal advocacy networks were also cited as important protective factors. Participants emphasized the need for expanded nonprofit support, referral networks for affirming providers, and increased local access to culturally competent care.


13.1.6 Veterans
Veteran participants discussed health primarily through the lens of access, continuity of care, and system navigation. A healthy life was described as one that includes timely medical care, mental health support, and the ability to successfully navigate Veteran-specific healthcare and benefits systems. Participants acknowledged the availability of Veteran services but identified challenges related to enrollment, awareness, and coordination between federal, state, and local systems. Mental health care was identified as a significant unmet need. Some participants expressed uncertainty about eligibility for services or concerns about taking resources away from other Veterans, highlighting the persistence of misinformation and stigma. Food insecurity and affordability were also identified as sources of stress, particularly in the context of rising costs of living. Participants identified access to outdoor spaces and recreational resources, such as the Heritage Trail, as positive contributors to health and well-being. However, transportation barriers and limited local access to services were noted as ongoing challenges. Veterans expressed a desire for stronger coordination between Veteran-serving organizations and community health systems, as well as expanded mental health resources outside of the VA system.


13.1.7 African American Faith-Based Organization (AME Zion)
Participants from an African American faith-based organization described health as encompassing physical, mental, spiritual, and community well-being. Access to basic needs such as healthy food, safe housing, and quality sleep were identified as foundational to health. Participants noted that community violence and safety concerns limit opportunities for physical activity, particularly for children. Key challenges identified included the high cost of housing and food, low wages relative to the cost of living, and limited access to affordable childcare and public transportation. Participants emphasized that these economic pressures create chronic stress that negatively affects health across the lifespan. Historical mistrust of healthcare systems and experiences of bias were also identified as ongoing barriers to care. Faith-based institutions were highlighted as trusted community anchors that play a critical role in health education, resource sharing, and social support. Participants emphasized the importance of culturally responsive care and stronger partnerships between public health agencies and faith-based organizations to address longstanding disparities and improve health outcomes within the community.

title: 13  Community Input
text:
13.2 LGBTQ+ Survey
In 2023 and 2024, the Orange County Department of Health (OCDOH) conducted an LGBTQ+ community survey at a variety of local LGBTQ+ events, including Pride celebrations and other community gatherings, as part of an effort to better understand the identities, healthcare experiences, and health concerns of LGBTQ+ residents. Hosting the survey in these community-centered spaces was a deliberate strategy to engage with LGBTQ+ individuals beyond those who may already seek services from the health department or traditional healthcare systems. By meeting people where they are, OCDOH sought to capture a broader range of perspectives and ensure that the voices reflected in the findings represent the diversity of the community itself.
Findings from the survey illustrate the diversity of identities within the LGBTQ+ community and a wide range of healthcare experiences. While some participants described positive and affirming interactions with providers, others reported feeling misunderstood, uncomfortable, or hesitant to disclose their identity in healthcare settings. These differing experiences suggest that access to inclusive and affirming care is not consistent across the county.
A common theme across responses was the need for greater awareness, education, and sensitivity among healthcare providers related to LGBTQ+ health. Participants emphasized the importance of respectful communication, correct use of names and pronouns, and provider knowledge of LGBTQ+-specific health concerns. When these elements are present, individuals are more likely to feel safe seeking care and to maintain ongoing relationships with providers.
The survey results show the diversity within the LGBTQ+ community and the unique challenges they face in healthcare. By using these insights, we can work towards better healthcare experiences and outcomes for LGBTQ+ individuals. A complete list of the survey questions and answers are included in Appendix A.

title: 13  Community Input
text:
13.3 Community Asset Survey

13.3.1 Overview
The Orange County Department of Health (OCDOH) developed a Community Asset Survey (CAS) as part of the 2025 Community Health Assessment (CHA) to assess residents’ perceptions of community strengths, areas for improvement, and prominent health issues affecting Orange County. The CAS was designed to capture resident perspectives that complement quantitative health indicator data and provide additional context regarding community conditions and lived experiences.
The survey began with two demographic questions asking respondents whether they lived in Orange County and to provide their ZIP code. Three primary questions followed, asking residents to choose from a list:

What are the greatest strengths of our community?
Where should the community focus its resources and attention to improve the quality of life in our community?
What are the most important health issues that our community should focus on?

For each question, respondents were able to select up to three responses, as well as provide open-ended feedback through an “Other” option. A complete list of survey questions and answers is included in Appendix B.


13.3.2 Methodology
The Community Asset Survey was developed and administered from April 29-August 31, 2025. The survey was distributed countywide and was available to residents through an online platform accessible via QR code and direct link. The survey was offered in English and Spanish. All responses were collected anonymously.
A convenience sampling approach was used to collect responses. Recognizing that online surveys may underrepresent certain populations, OCDOH monitored response patterns throughout the data collection period and implemented targeted outreach efforts to increase participation among underrepresented ZIP codes and populations. Community partners, including healthcare providers, schools, municipalities, libraries and community-based organizations, all who assisted in disseminating the survey to residents, staff, and clients. Additionally, in-person surveys were administered at community events including National Night Out, farmer’s markets, health screenings, community days, and food pantries.


13.3.3 Results
A total of 1,104 surveys were submitted. Respondents who indicated that they do not live in Orange County were excluded from the final sample. Respondents who lived in Orange County but only completed the demographic questions were also removed. All respondents who completed at least one question beyond the demographic section were included in the final analysis. After applying these criteria, 1,051 survey responses were included in the analysis.
For each survey question, respondents were able to select up to three responses from a predetermined list and could provide additional feedback through an “Other” response. During data analysis, all “Other” responses were reviewed individually.


13.3.4 Zip Code Representation
OCDOH targeted specific ZIP codes in its convenience sample, with the goal of achieving a distribution of responses that approximate the Orange County population. Using U.S. Census American Community Survey (ACS) 5-Year population estimates for Orange County (403,840 residents), the ten most populated ZIP codes in the county represent approximately 61–62% of the total county population, and a comparable proportion of Community Asset Survey (CAS) responses originated from these ZIP codes (66.2%).
Among the most populated ZIP codes, the largest shares of Orange County residents live in 10950 (Monroe), 12550 (Newburgh), and 10940 (Middletown). Monroe residents were underrepresented in the CAS sample, comprising approximately 16.2% of the county population but only 4.3% of survey respondents. Newburgh residents were slightly overrepresented, accounting for approximately 13.6% of the county population and 15.9% of survey respondents. Middletown residents were slightly underrepresented, comprising approximately 13.1% of the county population and 12.2% of survey respondents.
There were some ZIP codes without any representation in the CAS sample, including Bellvale (10912), Howells (10932), New Milford (10959), Southfields (10975), Sterling Forest (10979), Thompson Ridge (10985), West Point (10996 and 10997), Vails Gate (12584), and Godeffroy (12739). Table 13.2 includes a complete list of ZIP code responses and representation in the CAS. A small number of respondents reported ZIP codes outside the Orange County ZIP code list; these responses were retained in the CAS dataset given self-reported Orange County residency.

13.3.4.1 “WHAT ARE THE GREATEST STRENGTHS OF OUR COMMUNITY?”
Following two demographic questions, the third question in the Community Asset Survey (CAS) asked respondents, “What are the greatest strengths of our community?” Respondents were able to select up to three responses from a predetermined list, as well as provide written feedback if their response was not listed as an option.
The top five selected community strengths identified by Orange County residents were access to good education (340), parks and recreation (301), access to basic healthcare (251), low crime and safe neighborhoods (247), and access to affordable and healthy food (162) Figure 13.1. Other commonly identified strengths included a clean environment (152), a bike-able and walk-able community (142), and arts and cultural events (123).
Fewer respondents identified good jobs and the local economy (66), affordable housing (59), respect for all people (53), and low violence and abuse (37) as key community strengths. Good public transportation (28) was the least frequently selected strength.
When residents provided written responses outside of the pre-selected options, recurring themes included appreciation for the county’s natural surroundings and quality of life, community events such as farmer’s markets, and mutual support among residents.
“WHERE SHOULD THE COMMUNITY FOCUS EFFORTS TO IMPROVE QUALITY OF LIFE?”
The next question in the Community Asset Survey (CAS) asked respondents, “Where should the community focus efforts to improve quality of life?” Respondents were able to select up to three responses from a predetermined list, as well as provide written feedback if their response was not listed as an option.
The top five selected areas for improvement identified by Orange County residents were more affordable housing (360), better jobs and the local economy (303), improved public transportation (207), access to basic healthcare (177), and more programs, activities, and support for youth and teens during non-school hours (163). Fewer respondents selected more access to help during times of stress and crisis (79), lower violence and abuse (domestic, elder, child) (65), more parks and recreation (57), and more religious or spiritual values (29) as top areas for improvement. When residents wrote in responses that were not on the pre-selected list, recurring themes were: road maintenance, traffic and infrastructure, and senior programs and housing. Figure 13.2

Figure 13.2: Number of Responses to the Question: “Where should the community focus its resources and attention to improve the quality of life in our community?”


                            
                                            






13.3.4.2 “WHAT ARE THE MOST IMPORTANT HEALTH ISSUES OUR COMMUNITY SHOULD FOCUS ON?”
The final question in the Community Asset Survey (CAS) asked residents, “What are the most important health issues our community should focus on?” Respondents were able to select up to three responses from a predetermined list, as well as provide written feedback if their preferred responses were not listed as options.
The top five identified health issues among Orange County residents were mental health (depression, anxiety, stress) (258), drug use (prescription and illegal) (243), aging-related problems (Alzheimer’s disease, arthritis, hearing and vision loss, etc.) (204), homelessness (173), and safe, affordable, and adequate housing (166) (see Figure 154). Fewer respondents identified high blood pressure (22) infectious diseases (COVID-19, hepatitis, tuberculosis, etc.) (19), respiratory and lung diseases (13), sexually transmitted diseases (HIV and other STIs) (9), and teenage pregnancy (7) as top health issues.
When residents provided written responses outside of the pre-selected options, recurring themes included concerns related to affordability, environmental conditions, access to healthcare services, inclusivity, and awareness and support for individuals with developmental disabilities.
Residents’ responses to the most important health issues were categorized by the Prevention Agenda 2025-2030 priority areas Figure 13.4. Most responses fell into the domain of “Social and Community Context” (36.1%), with the concerns of mental health, substance use, suicide, and healthy eating as the most pressing issues. Nearly 20% of responses fell outside of the Prevention Agenda domains with residents listing aging problems (Alzheimer’s, arthritis, loss of hearing/vision), child abuse and neglect, domestic violence, heart disease and stroke, and infectious diseases as top concerns. Nearly 18% of responses fell within the domain of “Health Care Access & Quality”, with top concerns including cancer, obesity, lack of access to health care, and dental issues. Issues within the domain of Economic Stability included homelessness, safe and affordable housing and hunger, which accounted for 16.5% of responses.
Overall, CAS responses indicate that residents view behavioral health, substance use, housing stability, aging-related needs, and community safety as priority areas for improving health and well-being in Orange County.

13.3.4.3 Survey Responses by ZIP Code and Geographic Classification
Although many of the same themes were present throughout the county, survey responses revealed that each community is unique and may have different needs to address overall health. To enable the analysis of survey responses by geographic region, zip codes were classified using the US Department of Agriculture’s rural-urban commuting area (RUCA) codes, which were developed based on population size, population density, and daily commuting patterns (Insert link to the definition). For the purpose of analysis, RUCA codes were combined into three categories using a pre-existing consolidation scheme that incorporates the concept of residents’ potential access to services and resources.7 Following this scheme, zip codes were labeled as either “urban core”, “suburban”, or “large rural”. Urban core is defined as a contiguous built-up area of 50,000 people or more, suburban includes areas with 30% or more of their commuting follows to urban cores, and large rural describes towns with populations of 10,000 to 49,999 and surrounding rural areas with 10% or more of primary commuting to these towns/secondary commuting flows of 10% or more to urban cores.
There were key differences in the responses between urban core, suburban, and large rural communities. Respondents from urban core areas were less likely to identify affordable housing, parks and recreation, and support for youth and teens during non-school hours as a strength compared to those from suburban and large rural areas. Arts and cultural events, and programs, activities, and support for senior communities were more likely to be identified by large rural communities than urban core or suburban communities. Low crime and safe neighborhoods and clean environment were dominant strengths in suburban communities (See Figure 154).
Opinions on where resources should be focused to improve quality of life also differed by geographic classification. Compared to suburban and urban core communities, large rural areas were more likely to prioritize jobs and the economy, access to good education, and more programs, activities, and support for youth and teens during non-school hours. Suburban communities place more focus on more affordable housing, improved access to affordable and healthy food, and access to basic health care. Compared to large rural and suburban residents, respondents from urban core communities were more likely to prioritize parks and recreation, lower crime and safer neighborhoods, improving respect for all people, and more religious or spiritual values (See Figure 154).
There were also some geographic differences in community perceptions of the most important health issues. Mental health and drug use were the most identified health issues overall, with suburban communities selecting these health issues slightly more than those from urban core and large rural areas. Homelessness, alcohol use, hunger, and tobacco and vaping were issues more frequently identified by residents from urban core areas. Safe and affordable housing, suicide, and mental illness were more commonly identified by suburban residents compared to other communities. Residents from large rural communities identified gun violence, aging problems, physical inactivity, and lack of walkability more often than residents from other communities (See Figure 154).
Differences were also found when examining respondents from zip codes within each geographic classification. For example, Monroe, Middletown, and Newburgh are all classified as urban core areas, but Newburgh identified more affordable housing and lower crime and safer neighborhoods as two of the top three areas to focus resources, while Monroe and Middletown had the same two of the top three areas: improving respect for all people and a cleaner environment. See the ZIP code results for a complete list of the top three responses for each survey question by zip code. For the purposes of small sample sizes, only the top 10 zip codes with the most responses are included in the table.
7 Washington State of Department of Health, 2016, https://doh.wa.gov/sites/default/files/legacy/Documents/1500/RUCAGuide.pdf, accessed February 2026


13.3.4.4 Survey Comparisons Between 2022 and 2025 Responses
To compare responses from the same survey administered in 2022, dot plot graphs and 95% confidence intervals were calculated. Survey questions and response options were based on prior editions of this survey conducted in 2022. Dot plot graphs were created to compare three of the five survey questions including community strength perceptions, community priorities to improve quality of life, and community perceptions on the most important health issues. Survey results are presented here as unweighted percentages of respondents who took the survey in 2022 compared to percentages of respondents who took the survey in 2025. Estimates are displayed within a 95% confidence interval, the width of which represents the uncertainty in the estimate and depends on the proportion of respondents, the population size, the sample size, and the confidence level. The dots represent the percentage estimate for each question while the confidence intervals are expressed as a bar through the dot. The difference in estimates between 2022 and 2025 survey responses were considered statistically significant if the confidence interval bars do not overlap.
When comparing the community strength perceptions between 2022 and 2025, there were six areas where there was a statistical difference between the estimates. All six were deemed a greater strength of their community in 2022 compared to 2025 (Figure 156). The six areas included access to good education, parks and recreation, access to basic health care, low crime and safe neighborhoods, a clean environment, and respect for all people. Respondents completing the survey in 2025 chose many of the same priority areas to improve quality of life compared to 2022. There were also six statistically significant differences between survey responses in the two years. Respondents ranked access to affordable and healthy foods, programs, activities, and support for the senior community, programs, activities and support for youth and teens during non-school hours, good jobs and economy, affordable housing, and low violence and abuse lower than in 2022 when asked where resources should be focused to improve quality of life in Orange County (Figure 157). Respondents also chose “other” more in 2022, but data analysis of written responses did not reveal any themes. When asked to provide the top three health priorities in Orange County, responses from 2022 and 2025 were nearly identical. Only three health priorities were ranked higher in 2022 compared to 2025 (Figure 158). These priorities included mental health (depression, anxiety, stress), drug use (prescription and illegal), and infectious diseases (COVID, hepatitis, TB). Homelessness was also found to be statistically different from 2022, but it was ranked higher in 2025.

13.4 Resident Priority Selection
As part of engaging the broader community to participate in the selection of priority areas, OCDOH invited residents to engage in a one-question online survey. Residents were asked: ’Which of the following health problems in Orange County would you fix first?” Participants were asked to select one priority from the following list: alcohol and drug use, cancer, people not getting enough exercise, people not having enough food to eat, and suicide. These five priority areas were chosen through the OC Summit Planning Committee when all data were reviewed from various health assessments including secondary data sources, primary data sources such as the Community Provider Survey, Community Health Survey, Community Asset Survey, focus groups, and key informant interviews and analysis from the Orange County Health Summit. This survey was shared through OCDOH social media as well as through partner organizations such as hospitals, community-based organizations, other County government departments and municipalities. Five hundred seventy-six people participated in the survey from November 12- December 16, 2025. The top three priority areas that residents voted for were: People not having enough food to eat (40.1%), alcohol and drug use (26.9%), and cancer (15.3%). title: 13  Community Input

13.5 Community Health Survey

13.5.1 Introduction
The Siena College Research Institute (SCRI), on behalf of the Orange County Health Department, conducted a public opinion survey of 900 Orange County, NY residents from May 20 - June 26, 2024. Residents aged 18 and older were interviewed from within Orange County in New York State so as to ensure a representative county-wide sample. In addition to the county-wide sample, oversamples of Latino(a/é), Black/African-American and low SES households were collected to enhance statistical representativeness. In 2018 and 2022, SCRI conducted a similar survey for the seven counties in the Mid-Hudson Region. Orange County also conducted the survey in 2023 and again in 2024. Samples from 2018, 2022, 2023, and 2024 were similarly weighted to the most current demographic estimates and, as such, can be fairly compared to one another.
While the 2024 survey is summarized here, the Community Health Survey Dashboard8 provides access to all longitudinal data and can be accessed via the OCDOH website.


13.5.2 Methodology and Design
Within Orange County, a total of 900 residents aged 18 and older completed the survey. The margin of error for the total sample of 900 is +/- 3.8% including the design effects resulting from weighting with a 95% confidence interval. There was a total of 800 respondents who completed the survey through a dual frame (landline and cell phone) mode, and 100 who completed the survey via the online panel (Lucid). The county-wide sample of 900 was weighted by age, gender, reported race/ethnicity, income and county using the 2015-2020 American Community Survey 5-year estimates to ensure statistical representativeness. For a more in-depth breakdown of the Siena Survey Tool see Appendix D.

A Master sheet - the roster of every indicator (Activate/Deactivate, Object_Type, Indicator Name, Object ID, Figure ID, data source).
A Dropdowns sheet - reference lists for the data-entry dropdowns (format codes, y-labels, sources, dates, …).
One sheet per indicator with a config block in columns A/B (Name, Table/Figure/Both, Object ID, Figure Type, X Column, …) and the data entered to the right of the Enter Data cell.













NoteSource





NYS Community Health Indicator Reports Dashboard, August 2025 sourced from US Census Bureau, Small Area Income and Poverty Estimates https://webbi1.health.ny.gov/SASStoredProcess/guest?_program=%2FEBI%2FPHIG%2Fapps%2Fchir_dashboard%2Fchir_dashboard& p=ch&cos=33









Note



Note: This includes the population who live below the federally determined guidelines for poverty.

title: 14  Template Example: Live Data Objects
text:
14.2 To add your own indicator

Copy an indicator sheet (Poverty Rate or Total Households).
Set the config cells in column A/B - especially Name, Table/Figure/Both (figure or table), Object ID, and (for figures) Figure Type / X Column.
Fill the data to the right of the Enter Data cell: the row-label column (col F) plus value columns, with per-column format codes in the row just above.
Add the indicator to the Master roster (optional, for tracking).
Reference it in any chapter with {{< include _generated/objects/<object_id>.qmd >}} (e.g. fig-<id> or tbl-<id>), run the generator once, then quarto render.

See scripts/WORKBOOK_SCHEMA.md and scripts/PIPELINE_USAGE.md for full details.
